scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Bigwala is an ancient ceremonial music and dance form of the Basoga, a Bantu-speaking community in southeastern Uganda near Mt.
Elgon and Lake Victoria.
Oral tradition traces the practice to at least the 18th century, with origins linked to Kintu, who brought gourd trumpets from Mt.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically used for royal coronations, anniversaries, and funerals of Busoga kings (*Kyabazinga*), Bigwala also serves broader social functions.
It facilitates community bonding, courtship, and collective mourning when a fellow player dies.
Lyrics narrate Basoga history, reconfirm royal lineage, and convey social ethics regarding leadership and marriage.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The performance is structured as a cumulative procession.
A solo trumpet opens the piece, followed in succession by four interlocking hocket trumpets, five drummers, singers, and processional dancers.
Dancers move in a widening circular formation around the central drummers.
Watch for Waist Sway, Processional Hop.

Formation: Concentric circular processional line rotating around central drummers, gradually widening as participants join.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is produced by a set of five monotone side-blown gourd trumpets (*Bigwala*) tuned to a pentatonic scale (F, G, A, C, D).
The ensemble features *Enhana* (lead/deepest tone in triple or quadruple meter), *Empala*, *Endhasasi*, *Endesi*, and *Endumirizi* (highest tone).
Listen for the Enhana (gourd trumpet), Empala (gourd trumpet), Endhasasi (gourd trumpet), Endesi (gourd trumpet).
The pulse is 4/4 or 3/4 at about 103 beats a minute.

A dense, interlocking texture of five single-note side-blown gourd trumpets playing rapid pentatonic hocket patterns over a heavy, layered five-drum rhythmic foundation, accompanied by call-and-response vocals and high-pitched ululations.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Bigwala is performed in open palace courtyards (*Lubiri*) or village meeting spaces.
Performers wear traditional Basoga garments designed to emphasize waist articulation.

Gourd trumpets (*Enhendo*) are hand-crafted by harvesting long-necked gourds, smoke-curing them on heat racks (*Ekibani*) above fireplaces for a month, sectioning them into *Ebidome*, joining pieces with ant-nest glue or *Lukone* tree sap, and cutting side mouthpieces.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include King Henry Wako Muloki; master bearers and players Otuli Kakolokombe, James Lugolole, Lugolole Muyaga, Tomasi Tigaghalana, Sulayi Maganda Kifembe, and Kasadha Myenge Kakaire; educator Arthur Musulube; and promoter Godfrey Alibatya.

Busoga Bigwala shares strong technical and historical resemblances to Buganda trumpet traditions, as well as royal processional trumpet dances of neighboring groups, including the *Empango* of the Banyoro and the *Agwara* of the Lugbara people.
Bigwala sits within the Bantu ceremonial and royal court tradition of East Africa.
